label: Roadmap
notes: Open by naming the unifying move: the chapter studies spaces built by declaring old points indistinguishable and then asking which topology is forced. The lecture route follows the notebook rather than the page layout: partitions, projection maps, neighborhood tests, invariant ledgers, group quotients, and orbit spaces. Emphasize that every later construction is a controlled form of forgetting.

label: Partitions Become Points
notes: Use this slide to separate two ideas students often merge. First, the quotient set is easy: every part of the partition becomes a point. Second, the quotient topology is the real mathematical content. It is defined through the projection map, so the class picture only becomes a topological space after preimages are used as the open-set test.

label: Mobius Strip From Rectangle
notes: Present the Mobius strip as the chapter's first laboratory, not as a surface students already know. The rectangle is the source space, and the half-twist rule is the partition data. The seam point downstairs has two representatives upstairs, so a neighborhood near that point must be tested in both places at once. This prepares the quotient topology slide.

label: Quotient Topology Test
notes: This is the most important local test in the lecture. Ask students to inspect the glued endpoint on the circle and then look upstairs at the two interval ends. The visible neighborhood downstairs has a two-piece preimage. The artifact check records that one endpoint piece alone is not saturated, which is why quotient openness cannot be read from only one representative.

label: Continuity Out Of Quotient
notes: Explain this as the quotient's universal measuring device. To prove a function out of a quotient is continuous, we avoid guessing what open sets look like downstairs. We compose with the projection and test on the familiar source. Stress the extra well-definedness step: points identified by q must receive the same value under the proposed function.

label: Identification-Map Criteria
notes: Frame this slide as a practical checklist for examples. A continuous onto map need not automatically carry the quotient topology, so the chapter supplies criteria. If the map is open or closed, it is an identification map. If the source is compact and the target is Hausdorff, closedness comes for free, making many geometric quotient models legitimate.

label: Standard Quotient Models
notes: Use the gallery to insist that quotient drawings are recipes, not final evidence. Each model starts with a source object and a rule that says which boundary or interior points become equal. The same recipe can be embedded or drawn differently, so the lecture tracks invariant consequences such as orientability, boundary components, Euler characteristic, and local seam behavior.

label: Glueing And Attaching
notes: Connect glueing to quotients rather than treating it as a separate lemma. The disjoint union keeps the pieces honest, and the identification map records exactly which boundary or overlap points are equal. The continuity statement then becomes another instance of the quotient continuity test: if each piece behaves correctly and the overlaps agree, the assembled map behaves correctly.

label: Projective Space Descriptions
notes: Projective space is the deck's best example of comparing descriptions. The lecture should not ask students to memorize three definitions as unrelated facts. Each description has the same equivalence classes seen from a different source. Use the compact-to-Hausdorff criterion to explain why concrete maps can prove these descriptions produce homeomorphic quotient spaces.

label: Edge Invariant Ledger
notes: Treat this table as the ledger that keeps pictures accountable. The quotient rule is the input, but the invariant columns record what the rule forces. Have students compare the cylinder and Mobius strip: both have Euler characteristic zero, yet boundary count and orientability separate them. Then compare the torus and projective-style disk model: both are closed, but orientability and Euler characteristic separate them.

label: Surface Seam Inspection
notes: This slide is an instructional handoff to the interactive surface view. Explain what students should inspect before opening it: the cylinder closes with matching transverse coordinate, the Mobius strip closes only when that coordinate is reversed, and the torus is periodic in both directions. The numerical errors are not proofs by themselves, but they confirm that the rendered models follow the quotient recipes.

label: Topological Groups
notes: Topological groups give quotients extra structure because algebraic translations are homeomorphisms. Begin with the real line modulo integer translation, since the exponential map shows exactly which points are identified. Then point out that the same map respects the group operation: addition modulo integers becomes multiplication on the circle. The displayed checks are numerical witnesses for that compatibility.

label: Matrix Groups And Spheres
notes: Move from the circle quotient to matrix quotients. Orthogonal matrices act on the sphere by sending a unit vector to another unit vector. The action is transitive, so the orbit of e1 is the whole sphere. The stabilizer of e1 is a lower-dimensional orthogonal group. That stabilizer is precisely what is divided out in the homogeneous-space description.

label: Orbit Space Definition
notes: Define orbit spaces after students have already seen several quotient examples. The important conceptual shift is that the equivalence relation is now generated by homeomorphisms. Representatives are useful for drawing, but the quotient point is the entire orbit. This distinction matters in later examples, where two actions of the same group on the same space can produce different orbit spaces.

label: Same Group Different Quotients
notes: Use this slide to prevent a common overgeneralization. Knowing the acting group is not enough to know the quotient. The source span describes several actions of a two-element group on a torus, producing different quotient spaces. The difference is how the generator moves the torus and how the chosen fundamental piece has its boundary identified.

label: Dense And Closed Orbits
notes: This is the strongest warning that orbit representatives can mislead. In the square picture the irrational flow keeps jumping across identified edges, so it appears as many line segments. On the torus it is one orbit, and it is dense without being the whole torus. Contrast it with a rational slope, where the orbit closes and covers far fewer grid cells in the notebook diagnostic.

label: Fundamental Regions And Recap
notes: Close by returning to the big rule. A fundamental region is a convenient representative system, not the quotient itself. Its boundary records the missing identifications. The final checklist connects the lecture back to the notebook: artifacts exist, endpoint and seam identities were checked, group quotient identities were tested, and irrational orbit sampling behaved differently from the rational orbit.
